item.title: confoundvis for Visualizing and Reporting Sensitivity to Unmeasured Confounding in R
item.description: arXiv:2610.13731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sensitivity analysis asks how strong unmeasured confounding would have to be before an observational conclusion changes. Established methods answer this question using different quantities, including partial $R^2$ values, correlation products, and risk ratios. In this article, we present confoundvis, an R package that organizes these results through a common object, plotting functions, and reports. It calculates partial $R^2$ and impact-threshold paths from fitted linear models, imports results from sensemakr, konfound, and EValue, and provides measured-covariate benchmarks for the OLS frameworks. We demonstrate the workflow with 5,735 patients from the right heart catheterization study. The adjusted linear probability coefficient is 0.0634, the point-null robustness value is 0.0608, and the conditional significance impact threshold is 0.0376. The largest adverse leave-one-term-out measured-covariate product is 0.0090. Because the benchmark and threshold use different conditioning sets, their ratio is descriptive. A separate modified Poisson model gives a risk ratio of 1.103 and an E-value of 1.439. The contribution is a software workflow that keeps each method's units and decision rule clear. The package is available from CRAN.
item.dc:creator: Subir Hait

item.title: Product Monte Carlo: Expectation Under a Product of Densities
item.description: arXiv:2610.12702v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Aggregating independently computed sub-sample inferences is a well-known challenge in large-scale Bayesian computation, federated learning, and opinion pooling. The core problem is to approximate a distribution whose density is proportional to a product of individual densities. We propose Product Monte Carlo (PMC), an algorithm for computing arbitrary expectations under a product of densities using only Monte Carlo draws from individual densities. We turn the intractable product expectation into a regression problem by expressing it through a family of computable conditional expectations. Besides the point estimate, our fully Bayesian regression formulation provides coherent uncertainty quantification and principled diagnostics. We establish theoretical guarantees on consistency and characterize convergence rates for the PMC estimator. Across simulated and real-data experiments varying the number, dimensionality, and heterogeneity of the component distributions, PMC achieves higher estimation accuracy, better-calibrated uncertainty coverage, and improved scalability at a lower computational cost than existing methods. In addition, PMC requires no density evaluation, making it applicable to simulation-based inference, as we demonstrate in an application with protein images.
item.dc:creator: Pietro Carlotti, Sifan Liu, Yuling Yao

item.title: Two-way Guidance: Simultaneous Learning of Summary Statistics for Generative Bayes
item.description: arXiv:2610.12850v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Bayesian simulation-based inference (SBI) can struggle to recover increasingly concentrated posteriors as observation size grows. We consider learning sufficient summary statistics jointly with the posterior as a general principle for scalable inference in various SBI methods. A common measure taken in SBI is dimension reduction through predetermined summaries, which may partially discard posterior information. Our approach instead imposes structure on how the posterior learner depends on a learned summary (e.g., affinity), and learns the summary simultaneously with the posterior. We identify an important mechanism named two-way guidance: under a structural restriction on the summary, the posterior sufficiency of the learned summary simplifies posterior learning, whereas a suitable posterior objective guides the learned summary towards posterior sufficiency. This mechanism explains a counterintuitive finding that the structural restriction on the summary statistics improves posterior learning, rather than limit its performance. We establish theoretical guarantees on both posterior estimation error and the learned summary's departure from sufficiency, thus identifying conditions on the simulation budget for recovering increasingly concentrated posteriors as observation size grows.
item.dc:creator: Percy S. Zhai, Max Pachman, Peverel D. Shipley, Jungeum Kim

item.title: Generalized Determinantal Point Processes for Attraction and Repulsion with Distinct Interaction Kernels
item.description: arXiv:2610.12894v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Determinantal point processes (DPPs) model subset selection probability with repulsion, but many applications also exhibit attraction arising from pairwise relations or shared latent structures. Nonsymmetric DPPs (NDPPs) capture both effects, but their kernels are difficult to interpret and specify. We propose the determinant-ratio point process (DRPP), which models repulsion and attraction via a ratio of the determinants of two symmetric positive-definite kernels. This formulation preserves the feature-based interpretation of standard DPPs while allowing the two effects to be specified separately. Furthermore, we introduce an auxiliary-variable representation that enables efficient MCMC sampling and yields tractable expectation formulas for key statistics including the normalizing constant, which together facilitate maximum-likelihood learning. We theoretically characterize the interaction structures well suited to DRPPs: for clustered attraction with $C$ latent groups, DRPPs exactly realize the target pairwise interactions with an attraction rank $C$, whereas NDPPs can require a rank that grows with the number of items given the same repulsion component. Conversely, nontransitive pair-specific attraction may require compensation through the DRPP repulsion kernel. Experiments support these predictions, showing that DRPPs fit transitive attraction with substantially fewer parameters than NDPPs.
item.dc:creator: Hideaki Ishibashi, Takahiro Kawashima, Hideitsu Hino

item.title: Spatial Prediction with Guided Diffusion
item.description: arXiv:2610.12967v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Spatial prediction is a critically important task in data analyses that involve spatially or spatio-temporally-referenced data. It is commonly carried out using hierarchical models, which comprise a process model describing the latent process of interest, and a data model describing how the process is observed. The target quantity is the predictive distribution, which is the conditional distribution of the latent spatial process given the observed data. Unfortunately, the predictive distribution is rarely available in closed form and can be difficult to sample from. Here, we show how recent developments in guided diffusion modelling from machine learning can address a wide class of problems in spatial prediction when the likelihood function derived from the data model is known and differentiable, possibly after relaxation. To show the versatility of the approach, we apply it to both Gaussian and non-Gaussian process models and a variety of data models that describe direct partial observations, linear and areal aggregates, counts, right censoring, and area-exceedance functionals. Where possible, we validate the framework against exact and Markov-chain-Monte-Carlo (MCMC)-derived predictive distributions. We demonstrate our approach on several simulation studies and in a controlled experiment of methane-flux inversion over the UK and Ireland. We show that guided diffusion can sample from the correct predictive distribution in a variety of settings, that it can be applied to models where MCMC is intractable, and that it scales well with the dimensionality of the latent process.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Zammit-Mangion, Lachlan Astfalck, Rapha\"el Huser, Christopher Nemeth, Henry B. Moss

item.title: Enhancing credit risk scorecards with transactional-based behavioural features
item.description: arXiv:2610.13199v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Background: Credit risk modelling is fundamental in financial institutions, typically using credit history, repayment behaviour, income, and outstanding debt to estimate a borrower's probability of default. Although transactional data are sometimes incorporated through aggregated measures such as recency, frequency, and monetary indicators, behavioural information embedded in raw transaction narratives remains largely unexplored due to its unstructured nature. This limits opportunities to extract richer behavioural insights. Aim: This research investigates payment narratives from transactional data as an alternative data source for credit risk modelling. Setting: The study uses transactional data from a large South African financial institution focused on small and medium enterprises. Method: Techniques such as natural language processing and regular expressions are used to transform unstructured transaction descriptions into meaningful, explainable behavioural features by categorising transactions into interpretable spending categories. A novel categorisation algorithm was developed and evaluated for classification accuracy. The extracted features are incorporated into a credit risk scorecard to assess their predictive value. Results: The categorisation algorithm demonstrates high classification accuracy. Using these features in the scorecard resulted in a significant increase in Gini compared to a scorecard without them. Conclusion: Text-based transactional information can be systematically extracted, categorised, and operationalised to enhance credit risk model performance. Contribution: The study develops a novel, integrated, explainable methodology for transforming transactional text into behavioural features, introduces a structured RegEx-based categorisation approach, and demonstrates their predictive value within traditional scorecard frameworks.
item.dc:creator: Dian Prinsloo, Tanja Verster, Neill Smit

item.title: Interval-valued circular time series: A toroidal score-driven approach with an application to wind direction
item.description: arXiv:2610.13642v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Circular data recorded over time, such as wind direction, are increasingly observed in intervals rather than as single point-valued observations, yet no existing framework accommodates data that are simultaneously circular, interval-valued, and temporally dependent. Time series models for point-valued circular data, including recently proposed score-driven approaches, assume that each observation is a single angle. This paper addresses this gap by proposing a dynamic conditional score framework for interval-valued circular time series. The lower and upper boundary sequences of the observed intervals are treated as circular time series governed by score-driven dynamics, which preserves the periodicity of the circular domain and the dependency of boundaries, in which the boundaries are coupled through a toroidal distribution and a jointly derived score. Maximum likelihood estimation is discussed, and their finite-sample performance is evaluated through simulation. An application to interval-valued wind direction data illustrates the practical value of retaining the interval structure within a fully rotationally invariant circular framework.
item.dc:creator: Thasmika Mohan, Najmeh Nakhaei Rad, Sphiwe Skhosana, Yaser Samadi

item.title: Scalable Sparse Autoregressive Variational Inference for Non-Gaussian Spatial Fields
item.description: arXiv:2610.13656v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Latent field models are essential for spatial statistics, but the posterior distribution of the latent field, even with a Gaussian process (GP) prior, is analytically intractable whenever the likelihood is non-Gaussian. Existing approximations are either too slow or too restrictive for large non-Gaussian datasets. We present a scalable variational inference framework that mirrors the sparse nearest-neighbor autoregressive structure of the prior in the variational family, uses normalizing-flow conditionals for expressiveness, and amortizes all variational parameters via a single shared neural conditioner. Doubly stochastic optimization with reduced ancestor sets achieves polylogarithmic complexity per iteration.
item.dc:creator: Paul F. V. Wiemann, Matthias Katzfuss

item.title: Estimation, Sensitivity Analysis, and Optimization of Distortion Risk Measures via Simulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.13751v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a simulation-based method for the estimation, sensitivity analysis, and optimization of distortion risk measures (DRMs), a class of performance measures that capture a wide range of risk attitudes through an underlying distortion function. Existing simulation approaches often approximate DRMs using numerical partitions or empirical distributions. We show that, when the distortion function is piecewise polynomial, the nonlinear structure of a DRM can be handled exactly, without introducing distortion discretization error, using only simulated system outputs. This representation enables the development of a computational method that integrates finite-difference techniques for sensitivity analysis and for solving a broad class of differentiable risk-based optimization problems. Under suitable conditions, we establish strong consistency and convergence rates for DRM estimation, sensitivity analysis, and optimization. We further extend the approach to non-polynomial distortion functions through polynomial approximation. Numerical experiments on synthetic and calibrated financial examples demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed approach across a range of applications.
item.dc:creator: Hao Cao, Jian-Qiang Hu, Jiaqiao Hu

item.title: bayprior: Structured Bayesian Prior Elicitation, Conflict Diagnostics, and Regulatory Reporting
item.description: arXiv:2609.16410v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bayesian clinical trials require a well-specified prior distribution, and regulators increasingly expect that specification to be documented, diagnosed for prior-data conflict, and shown to be robust to reasonable alternatives, yet few R tools connect the full workflow of prior construction, validation, and regulatory justification into a single package. We introduce bayprior, an R package and Shiny application that implements structured expert elicitation via quantile matching, moment matching, and the SHELF roulette method across six distribution families; linear and logarithmic expert opinion pooling with Bhattacharyya agreement diagnostics; derivation of meta-analytic-predictive (MAP) priors from historical trial data via random-effects meta-analysis; prior-data conflict assessment using the Box p-value, S-value (surprisal) surprise index, information divergence, Bhattacharyya overlap, and multivariate Mahalanobis distance; hyperparameter sensitivity analysis with tornado and influence heatmap visualisations; and robust, sceptical, and power prior alternatives. A regulatory reporting module generates self-contained HTML, PDF, or Word documents addressing expectations in the FDA's 2026 draft Bayesian methods guidance and in EMA guidance on incorporating external and historical information. The package is demonstrated on a synthetic oncology Phase II trial. bayprior is available on CRAN and includes a fully modular Shiny application for interactive use.
item.dc:creator: Ndoh Penn

item.title: Approximation of differential entropy in Bayesian optimal experimental design
item.description: arXiv:2510.00734v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Bayesian optimal experimental design provides a principled framework for selecting experimental configurations that maximize obtained information. In this work, we consider settings where the likelihood entropy is independent of the design or can be evaluated explicitly, which applies, e.g. to additive noise models with design-independent or explicitly computable noise entropy. This reduces the problem to maximum entropy estimation, where the nested integral defining the expected information gain collapses into a single integral. Our study is motivated by large-scale inference problems, such as inverse problems, where the computational cost is dominated by expensive likelihood evaluations. Under additive Gaussian noise model, we propose a computational approach in which the evidence density is approximated by a Monte Carlo or quasi-Monte Carlo surrogate, while the differential entropy is evaluated using standard methods without additional likelihood evaluations. We prove that this strategy achieves convergence rates that are comparable to, or better than, state-of-the-art methods for full expected information gain estimation, particularly when the cost of entropy evaluation is negligible. Our approach relies only on mild smoothness of the forward map and avoids stronger technical assumptions required in earlier work. We also present numerical experiments, which confirm some of our theoretical findings.
item.dc:creator: Chuntao Chen, Tapio Helin, Nuutti Hyv\"onen, Yuya Suzuki

item.title: SAT-sampling for statistical significance testing in sparse contingency tables
item.description: arXiv:2511.05709v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Exact conditional tests for contingency tables require sampling from fibers with fixed margins. Classical Markov basis MCMC is general but often impractical: computing full Markov bases that connect all fibers of a given constraint matrix can be infeasible and the resulting chains may converge slowly, especially in sparse settings or in presence of structural zeros. We introduce a SAT-based alternative that encodes fibers as Boolean circuits which allows modern SAT samplers to generate tables randomly. We analyze the sampling bias that SAT samplers may introduce, provide diagnostics, and propose practical mitigation. We propose hybrid MCMC schemes that combine SAT proposals with local moves to ensure correct stationary distributions which do not necessarily require connectivity via local moves which is particularly beneficial in presence of structural zeros. Across benchmarks, including small and involved tables with many structural zeros where pure Markov-basis methods underperform, our methods deliver reliable conditional p-values and often outperform samplers that rely on precomputed Markov bases.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Statistics and Computing, Volume 36, article number 229 (2026)
item.dc:creator: Patrick Scharpfenecker, Tobias Windisch

item.title: Reliability-Targeted Simulation of Item Response Data: Solving the Inverse Design Problem
item.description: arXiv:2512.16012v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Monte Carlo studies of item response theory (IRT) methods often leave the information level implicit in the choice of item parameters. Designs with the same sample size and test length can therefore represent quite different measurement conditions. We develop a calibration procedure that makes the information level an explicit design choice. The target is an information-based reliability index derived from population mean test information. Before generating responses, we solve for a common multiplier on item discriminations, keeping difficulties, test length and the reference population fixed. The R package IRTsimrel implements the procedure, allowing researchers to compare methods across chosen information levels or compare designs at a common target. In an item-level treatment-effect simulation, power increases across targets, while excess rejection from ignoring item-effect variation persists. These comparisons show how targeting helps distinguish findings that depend on the chosen information level from those that persist across the studied range.
item.dc:creator: JoonHo Lee

item.title: Particle-based Generalised Stochastic Optimisation
item.description: arXiv:2608.02844v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a class of general diffusion-based stochastic particle optimisation methods for loss functions with intractable gradients. Specifically, we consider problems in which the loss gradient is an integral with respect to a parameter-dependent distribution, a structure that includes training generative models, fine-tuning, and learning latent-variable models. We introduce mean-field dynamics and its interacting-particle approximations, which contain several existing algorithms as special cases and provide a route to constructing new methods. Under well-posedness and joint contractivity assumptions, we prove exponential convergence and show that the continuous-time particle system admits a non-asymptotic error bound. We illustrate our framework by developing higher-order Langevin and momentum optimisers and evaluating them on maximum marginal-likelihood estimation and energy-based-model training.
item.dc:creator: Jiechen Jackie Zhang, O. Deniz Akyildiz

item.title: Efficient quadratic entropy with distance sketches
item.description: arXiv:2610.11976v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We detail scalable methods for approximating the quadratic entropy $p^T d p$ for arbitrary distributions $p$ and common distances $d$ of negative type. We focus on the Euclidean and spherical geodesic cases, which both use random feature embeddings and projections to dramatically improve computational complexity within a simple framework. Amortization of a single large matrix multiplication and control variates further enable computation at large scale with low memory and runtime in situations where $d$ is held constant while $p$ varies. We demonstrate this with a comparison against direct pair sampling and bibliometric/scientometric examples on Open Graph Benchmark datasets, revealing papers, fields, and institutions with both particularly narrow and broad interdisciplinary reach from their citations and text features alone.
item.dc:creator: Steve Huntsman
